doc.title: Cascadu interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, November 15, 2019

chapter: Spirit, roots and the music's meaning
title: Yoruba songs, family priestesses and a global lineage
summary: He explains the vocal phrases as Trinidadian Yoruba tradition, his mother's priestess family, and his varied world percussion studies and ancestry.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: How did you learn the vocal phrases and melodies that I heard yesterday? That sounds like a long, seems like a long-term —

Some of that was from Trinidad tradition. And lot of it is — and it’s all Yoruba, right? So the tradition that, although there is Arara in Trinidad and there are Arara villages etcetera, this particular piece was Yoruba. And Trinidad was actually the patron saint of the island is Shango and the Shango “cult” quote unquote in Trinidad is a complete retention of the Yoruba presence, those divinities for the Africans who arrived in Trinidad. So I grew up with that stuff. My — I didn’t know, but my mother’s family was very, very close in the tradition. They were high priestesses in the tradition from my mother’s side of the family. And when I started becoming aware, they were the ones who were guiding me. It was those ancestors, I can identify them, that were guiding me altogether. And you know I realized that my path was one in which I had to really do — my life was about a journey of self discovery through the people who had come before me, so that much later on in life I went and found my father’s side of the family in Martinique, and in France and you know, I just started gathering information about who I was and where I came from. And I realized that, you know, the thing, it wasn’t just a curiosity. It was the music that led me there. Because as I got into the percussion world there were certain flavors that just meant so much to me. Everything, you know, you inject this color into the music as a percussionist. But I didn’t stay in one vein. I went into the Middle Eastern vein, I went into the North Indian and South Indian vein, I went into the Brazilian stuff. I went into the West African stuff. Yesterday I sat in on the West Africa class here and knew the pieces that they were playing: Agbekor and Gahu and everything else, vowed with Lydia to come back and you know, spend some time with the kids and everything else. Because I had studied that stuff. So I went into, I guess part of it is that I am the child of a confluence of global and traditional bloodlines. I am a product of the world, not of one group of people. I am a product of all kinds of bloodlines that have come together and the thing that helped me to discover that even more was the music. Because when I pick up a Middle Eastern tambourine and I play it, there’s something that is speaking to me. When I go to frame drums and I play frame drums and I study and I connect with people from Istanbul and from Syria and stuff. Because my grandfather on my mother’s side was Syrian-Lebanese. I never knew him. I never met him. But I remember distinctly when I discovered the percussive realm of the Middle East and Syria. I had — my grandfather came to me in a dream. And it didn’t happen — it didn’t happen until I had walked into that percussive realm.
Well this goes back to what we were talking about when we started today, this, what is it that that percussion music brings out of you.
I guess you can really speak to that.
